channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: New interactive map of Costa Rica showcases its cultural, natural and ocean heritage
item.description: PR Newswire: (PRESS RELEASE). “The platform brings together geographic, oceanographic, cultural, historical, and scientific information about the country, making knowledge about Costa Rica more accessible to students, teachers, researchers, domestic and international tourists, media outlets, and the general public. The information is available in both Spanish and English.”

item.title: Words of Bluesky
item.description: New to me, found on Bluesky, I think it launched about a year ago? “Look up an account to find the accounts that write about the same things, or search for words to find who uses them far more than most.” I looked up “database” to see which account was using that word the most and discovered it was the Wrestling Entrance Music Database.

item.title: The U.S. and Soviet versions of Reykjavik
item.description: National Security Archive: “President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev almost achieved a deal 40 years ago at the 1986 Reykjavik summit to abolish nuclear weapons, but the agreement would have required ‘an exceptional level of trust that neither side had yet developed,’ according to previously secret U.S. and Soviet documents posted on the Web by the National Security Archive of George Washington University.”

item.title: JewishGen revamps online database to help people uncover their family histories
item.description: CBS News: “[Karen] Lichtman’s discovery highlights the role of JewishGen, one of the world’s largest online resources for Jewish genealogy. Based at the Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York City, the organization is preparing to launch an updated website next week to help users navigate millions of historical records.”

item.title: Disney Inks Major Creator Deal With Dude Perfect
item.description: Hollywood Reporter: “Like Disney’s other creator deals, it will see some Dude Perfect content come to Disney+, including some of the group’s short-form library content. But it will also see the group create original content for its platforms and channels inspired by Disney events, with Super Bowl LXI, the 50th anniversary of Star Wars, and Marvel Studios’ Avengers: Doomsday among the projects being highlighted.”

item.title: TikTok says yes to more creator-led microdramas from Made By Us and HOORAE
item.description: Tubefilter: “As you probably know, ‘microdrama’ is the current format du jour for everyone hoping to make a buck in the entertainment industry, from Hollywood studios to major social media platforms. That includes TikTok, which just announced a new microseries-focused partnership with production company Made By Us Studios.”

item.title: The official Tom’s Hardware app is here — 30 years of tech coverage and benchmarks in your pocket
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “We’ve been sharing our passion for technology with you for 30 years, and today we’re introducing a faster, easier way to access all of our content while on the go. The official Tom’s Hardware app is live now, available for free on Android and iOS devices, bringing all of our content to your pocket in a clean, responsive application that is optimized for smartphones and tablets.”

item.title: When a Social Media Mob Came for Cornell’s Jane Doe
item.description: New York Times: “Within hours of Mr. Thompson’s post, another user had offered a bounty of $5,000 for the name and photos of the woman who had sued Cornell University under the pseudonym, claiming she had been gang raped at a fraternity party. Within a day, commenters were circulating a woman’s name and images of her from a social media account. On the fringes of the internet, bigots, attention-seekers and trolls have long seized on polarizing legal cases to air anger and disgust at women — and boost their following. Now they were coming for Jane Doe.”

item.title: US judge rebuffs $85 million fee request by lawyers in Google Play antitrust litigation
item.description: Reuters: ” A federal judge in California has rejected for now a request by lawyers for ​consumers who sued Alphabet’s Google over its Play Store practices to collect $85 million in legal fees from ‌a $630 million settlement, saying the attorneys failed to provide sufficient records to justify the award.”

item.title: My Quest for IndieWeb Citizenship
item.description: ilyess: “Browsing the internet, I landed on the IndieWeb site and went exploring that philosophy. I wasn’t new to the concept, but up until then I hadn’t taken the time to dig deep and really understand what it was all about. I knew it had to do with microformats — conventional HTML tags bloggers use to annotate information on their sites — and POSSE — which in practice for me means posting here first, then syndicating to Mastodon. But beyond that, I didn’t fully grasp the point. So I grabbed a cup of coffee and dove down the rabbit hole.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: New digital repository opens Pacific scholarship to the world
item.description: University of Auckland: This is more about the Pacific region (“Pacific Basin”) than the Pacific ocean. “Pacific research created at Waipapa Taumata Rau, University of Auckland is now more accessible than ever through the launch of Measina o le Pasefika, Treasures of the Pacific, a new digital repository designed to preserve, showcase and share Pacific scholarship with communities across Aotearoa and the wider Pacific….the repository brings together Pacific research in a searchable online platform, making it easier for students, academics, communities and future generations to discover, access and engage with Pacific knowledge.”

item.title: PayAuthors
item.description: Found in my RSS Feeds: It’s for writers to check and see if their books are being pirated. The check and initial list is free but if you want to make some futile attempt at protecting your intellectual property, you can get a full copyright registration report for a fee, I think $95. I ran a search and found lots of my books and one I had nothing to do with (“ActionScript 2.0 Garage”).

item.title: The Future of the Irish Republican Digital Archive
item.description: The Irish Republican Digital Archive: “With more than 7,100 documents now preserved on the Internet Archive, and the final collection expected to exceed 7,500, the Irish Republican Digital Archive has entered a new phase. The active digitising project has concluded, but the archive itself remains freely available. The following answers some of the questions people may have about the decision and what happens next.”

item.title: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
item.description: Reuters: “The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine ​for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter The officials said ‌leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.”

item.title: Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say
item.description: NiemanLab: “The new terms broadly cover business accounts that manage pages and groups, run advertisements, push marketing messages, and use the platform’s business account dashboard. As written, the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products, according to three legal experts who reviewed the terms at Nieman Lab’s request.”

item.title: BBC News launches live stream on YouTube in U.S., U.K.
item.description: TheDesk: “The British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) is hoping to expand the reach of its global news channel by bringing a live streaming simulcast of the network to YouTube in two key countries. Streamers in the United Kingdom and the United States can now watch the 24-hour BBC News feed via the BBC News YouTube channel, the broadcaster announced Thursday.”

item.title: Meta Withdraws $25 Million From Its Midterms Push
item.description: New York Times: “In the world of campaign finance, where outside groups often carry cash from cycle to cycle, returns of tens of millions of dollars are rare outside of scandals. Meta, one of the world’s largest and wealthiest companies, also does not need $25 million to add back to its cash reserves, which recently stood at more than $90 billion.”

item.title: Meta’s Smart Glasses May Have Been Recording People Without Their Knowledge
item.description: Gizmodo: “If you needed another reason to be skeptical of Meta’s smart glasses, congratulations—you can add ‘may record without my knowledge’ to the seemingly never-ending list. As noted by Android Authority, people who own Meta’s smart glasses have noticed that, after a recent firmware update, their smart glasses have been keeping records of some conversations even if they didn’t wake up the smart glasses’ voice assistant first.”

item.title: Attorney General Bonta Sues to Block Closure of San Francisco National Archives
item.description: State of California: “California Attorney General Rob Bonta today filed a lawsuit challenging the National Archives and Records Administration’s (NARA) abrupt decision to close the National Archives at San Francisco and transfer its holdings to other National Archives facilities across the country. The San Francisco National Archives holds records that tell the story of Northern and Central California’s history, with records dating back more than 175 years.”

item.title: The Internet’s undersea backbone is slipping into the danger zone
item.description: Ars Technica: “Despite the expansion of Starlink and other communications satellite services, most of the world’s Internet traffic still travels through subsea cables crisscrossing the ocean floors. Those fiber-optic cables coexist with a network of oil and gas pipelines and submarine power cables—and all these crucial links connecting countries and continents now face growing sabotage risks as gray-zone warfare and open conflicts have become widespread.”

item.title: Rare Korean books return to UH Mānoa after restoration
item.description: University of Hawaii: “Ten rare Korean books, including a historically significant military manual, have returned to the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s Hamilton Library following a year-long restoration project in South Korea. The books, severely damaged by water, insects and age, were restored by the Jungjae Cultural Heritage Conservation Institute in Seoul, one of Korea’s leading conservation laboratories. The collection includes military manuals, travelogues, poetry collections and Buddhist scriptures that had become nearly impossible for researchers to consult.”

item.title: Louvre could be forced to close without major overhaul, director warns
item.description: Euronews: “A year after thieves made off with €88 million of crown jewels that have never been found, the new man in charge says leaking pipes and crumbling galleries mean security fixes alone won’t save the Paris landmark.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: ACLU Marks the Supreme Court Term with New Digital Museum Experience Highlighting Landmark SCOTUS Cases
item.description: ACLU: “Today, the ACLU launched The People’s Archive, a dynamic digital museum that combines photography, audio, print, and video chronicling the organization’s key civil rights and civil liberties milestones throughout its over 100-year history.”

item.title: Wesley Hogan on preserving young people’s voices in the historical record
item.description: Duke University Libraries: “Dr. Wesley Hogan, is a Research Professor at the Franklin Humanities Institute and Department of History. Dr. Hogan has published the Youth Activists Oral Histories Collection within the Duke Research Data Repository (RDR). These oral histories were collected as part of Dr. Hogan’s Fall FOCUS Program class, ‘US Racial Justice and Environmental Justice Youth Movements since 2010.’ She shared with us her thoughts on partnering with Duke University Libraries to archive and share humanities data for future scholars.”

item.title: Hurricane Nolo’s path, rainfall impacts mapped in new interactive website
item.description: University of Hawaii: “The University of Hawaiʻi’s Hawaiʻi Climate Data Portal (HCDP) team has launched a new interactive website that allows the public to explore how Hurricane Nolo affected weather across the Hawaiian Islands, from its first rain bands over Hawaiʻi Island to the heavy rainfall that later drenched Kauaʻi and Oʻahu. Among the notable observations, Hawaiʻi Mesonet stations recorded storm rainfall totals exceeding 20 inches at three locations on Hawaiʻi Island, while a United States (U.S.) Geological Survey gauge at Mount Waiʻaleʻale on Kauaʻi recorded more than 38 inches.”

item.title: Double check your website’s alt texts with a bookmarklet
item.description: Juha-Matti Santala: “I built Alt text debugging bookmarklet (ATDB among friends as it rolls off the tongue nicely), a quick tool for website developers and authors to check the status of alt texts of images on a site. I use it daily with my own website and blog posts as a one last double check before I publish to make sure I didn’t forget to add alt texts to some images and that those that are decorative, have correct empty alt texts.”

item.title: Can YouTube’s €8.4 billion economic contribution get it a better deal in Europe?
item.description: Tubefilter: “For the second year in a row, YouTube has brought its Economic Impact Report across the pond. The eminent platform broke down its capital contributions across Europe as part of its effort to promote more harmonious dealings with continental regulators and media companies. The report claims that YouTube’s creator economy added €8.4 billion to the European gross domestic product (GDP) in 2025. That ecosystem supported more than 220,000 of what YouTube calls ‘full-time equivalent’ (FTE) jobs.”

item.title: When Slate went back to its 1996 homepage, it learned some web design lessons for 2026
item.description: NiemanLab: “The fonts are Times New Roman and Arial Narrow, the colors are maroon and mustard, and the cursor is the 8-bit pixel hand. When Slate revived its original 1996 homepage to celebrate its 30th birthday this fall1, the team found a lot to like besides nostalgia.”

item.title: U.S. Naval Academy Announces New School – Autonomous Systems
item.description: US Naval Academy: “The United States Naval Academy (USNA) announced a major academic restructuring today that will establish both a standalone school for computing, cybersecurity, super intelligence, robotics and autonomous systems and a standalone school of engineering.”

item.title: Blockbuster-era law governing privacy of video rentals gets a fresh look from the Supreme Court
item.description: Associated Press: “In 1988, Congress enacted a law to protect the privacy of video rentals after a journalist published details of Supreme Court nominee Robert Bork’s movie rental history during his Senate hearings. Nearly four decades later, the court is weighing how the Blockbuster-era statute fits into the modern age of digital commerce.”

item.title: ‘123456’ password linked to Denmark data breach affecting 8.8M people
item.description: The Register: “A person claiming responsibility for the breach of Denmark’s Central Register of Persons (CPR) says they gained access through an IT company’s account protected by the password ‘123456.’”

item.title: Yale Library ramps up digitization amid drop in physical item circulation
item.description: Yale Daily News: “Between 2016 and 2025, circulation of physical library materials through the Yale Library fell about 65 percent, from about 381,000 items in 2016 to about 132,000 items in 2025, according to Patricia Carey, the director of communications strategy for the library. Several librarians said they are looking to increase student engagement with library resources through increased digitization efforts.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Google says it needs the grid. The grid can’t keep up.
item.description: Politico: “Google is wrestling with its new role as an energy power player — one that’s thrust the tech giant into the world of arcane electric grid policy while it tries to defray the white-hot backlash against data centers. For a company that is driving the future of artificial intelligence, the slow pace of tapping into U.S. grids to power its data operations is its most threatening test, Marsden Hanna, Google’s head of energy and sustainability policy, told POLITICO’s Energy podcast.”

item.title: Elon Musk Tries to Convince Followers to Let Grok Control Their Credit Cards, in a Stunt That Immediately Backfires in a Very Embarrassing Way
item.description: Futurism: “Let Elon Musk never be accused of not leading by example. Last week, the world’s richest man sung the praises of his new Grok Bot AI agent, encouraging his followers to let it control their credit cards and shop for them.” Hilarity, as they say, ensued.

item.title: Inside Ohio’s Revolt Against Data Centers
item.description: Matter: “A four-hour legislative committee hearing in June, punctuated by applause and anger, offered a window into the growing backlash against data centers. The prospect of unchecked development has galvanized a cross-section of Ohioans, urban and rural, Democrat and Republican, alarmed about the spread of the giant computing facilities. Residents are demanding that local governments impose bans and moratoria on data centers while gathering signatures for a statewide ballot measure that could go before voters in 2027.”

item.title: Google defends Finnish forest clearance as building inspector faces dismissal
item.description: Helsinki Times: “Google has defended its decision to clear hundreds of hectares of forest for data centres in Finland before completing environmental assessments, claiming it believed authorities had agreed to the work. The dispute has also reached local government, where a senior building inspector has taken leave after alleging that she faced dismissal over comments to the media.”

item.title: El Paso and New Mexico spent millions on climate plans. Three new data centers could undo them.
item.description: Texas Tribune: “Last December, New Mexico officials celebrated publication of a plan to address climate change, designed to dramatically reduce the state’s greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. A few months later, just across the state line in Texas, El Paso city officials adopted their own such plan with a similar ambition. Each report cost millions of dollars to draft, but neither one took into account how the construction of data centers could upend climate goals in both places.”

item.title: Senators Question Meta’s Data Center Tax Strategy
item.description: New York Times: “In a letter to Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, seven Democratic senators, including Ron Wyden of Oregon, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, asked the company about $6.6 billion worth of federal research tax credits the company has claimed over the last two years.”

item.title: In a first for Delaware, Dover passes moratorium on data center development
item.description: Spotlight Delaware: “The Dover City Council on Monday unanimously approved a 18-month moratorium on the construction of data centers in Delaware’s capital city. The moratorium is the first of its kind in Delaware, and follows more than a year of discussions and debate across the state over how much the fast-growing industry could impact power bills and the local environment.”

item.title: Nicolas Cage Says He’s ‘Probably Not’ Working With Amazon Again After Refusing to Sign AI Waiver for ‘Spider-Noir,’ Teases Joining ‘True Detective’
item.description: Variety: “Nicolas Cage is speaking out against Amazon after the company, which developed ‘Spider-Noir’ for Prime Video, allegedly asked him to sign an AI waiver.”

item.title: Analysis: Google Is Poisoning Search Results For Rank Trackers
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “A new analysis from enterprise rank-tracking firm Nozzle claims that Google is showing misleading search results pages (SERPs) to rank trackers and AI companies in an apparent effort to poison the data they are attempting to collect.”

item.title: Behind AI industry’s call for independent reviews, a fight over what gets made public
item.description: Reuters: “Anthropic and OpenAI have sought significant control over what outside evaluators can publish, concerned that findings could reveal trade secrets, according to two people familiar with the discussions.”

item.title: SpaceX agrees to testify to NYC Council about AI safety after receiving subpoena
item.description: CNBC: “SpaceX has agreed to testify before the New York City Council this week as part of a legislative investigation concerning artificial intelligence safety risks, the council announced on Tuesday. The council said in a press release that the hearing will take place on Friday at 10 a.m. ET in front of its tech committee.”

item.title: The release of AI chatbots has harmed teens’ learning and Canada needs to act
item.description: The Conversation: “Two decades after the launch of social media, Meta settled a lawsuit in August in the United States about the negative impact of Facebook and Instagram on teens’ well-being. The company paid US$18 billion and agreed to limit teens’ access to prevent American government regulation. Just before this, in June, the Canadian government finally announced its own regulations, the Safe Social Media act, forcing platforms to remove harmful content. While better late than never, neither the American or Canadian intervention addresses AI chatbots. We should be concerned not only about about the effects of AI on teens’ safety, but also, as recent data from global standardized testing suggests, on teens’ learning.”

item.title: In the Kremlin’s AI Propaganda Blitz, the Noise Is the Signal
item.description: Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center: “Russia really is trying to influence the responses of global neural networks—primarily through the information they receive from the internet. Politicians, researchers, and journalists have known this for several years now. However, wanting to rewrite ChatGPT’s answer to the ‘who does Crimea belong to?’ question is one thing. Actually rewriting it is another. Before we can assess the effectiveness of the Kremlin’s AI propaganda ecosystem, we must first understand its diffuse, contradictory nature.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Number of data center fires and power failures has doubled since 2024
item.description: Data Center Dynamics: “According to the Energy Incident Register, which provides an independently run public register of safety incidents in energy and grid infrastructure, the number of fires or power failures at data centers rose from just eight in 2024 to 20 in 2025 and 19 in 2026. The Energy Incident Register now tracks data center incidents, based on public reporting, from 2010 to 2026 across 26 countries. Of 93 data center incidents in the period, 47 occurred in 2024 or later.”

item.title: Inside Out Library
item.description: Found in my RSS Feeds: From the About page: “1,800,189 public-domain pictures from 50,334 scanned books. Free to use, for anything. Old books are full of beautiful, strange, interesting illustrations, diagrams, and photographs. But unless you know which book to open, a lot of those pictures are hard to find. I wanted to make it easier to wander through them, find something unexpected, and see where it takes you.”

item.title: The Ukrainian project MetalScans has collected a digital archive of music press
item.description: From Neformat and machine-translated from Ukrainian: “The other day, the Metal Country Telegram channel announced the launch of the online project MetalScans , which collects and stores scanned copies of Ukrainian music magazines and zines.”

item.title: Big Thief Launch Live Archive
item.description: Clash: “James Krivchenia has a prevailing love of Grateful Dead live releases, and the manner in which that band encouraged bootleggers to record and share their concerts. As it grows, the Big Thief Live Archive will allow fans to build their own sets, creating playlists of their favourite live takes across the ever growing collection of live shows.”

item.title: Google Launches A Video Series For Odd Technical SEO Questions
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Google recently introduced ‘The Non-Canonical Cabinet,’ a Search Central YouTube series discussing edge case technical SEO issues. On Oct. 14, they published the first video of this new series, which addresses items that may and may not be included within a domain name or URL path (such as emojis) as well as whether using keywords within URLs affects search rankings.”

item.title: France’s Gen Alpha Revolution Was Built Over Snapchat
item.description: Teen Vogue: “At Bartholdi High School in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, the blockade started with a Snap. Jade, a junior, tells Teen Vogue that after news spread that students at other schools near Paris were gathering to protest, a girl in her class took to the app. ‘She said it was unacceptable for us to be living under these conditions at the high school. So, she started a [Snapchat] group with almost everyone from the school. That’s when we started protesting.'”

item.title: Setback for TikTok as EU court adviser backs gatekeeper label
item.description: Reuters: “An adviser to Europe’s highest court recommended on Thursday that TikTok lose its challenge to its ‘gatekeeper’ status under ​landmark EU rules, backing regulators in a closely watched test ‌of the bloc’s efforts to curb Big Tech’s power.”

item.title: Publishers Seek $19.5m From Pirate Library WeLib, Recycle Anna’s Archive Claims
item.description: TorrentFreak: “A group of major publishers has asked a New York federal court to issue a $19.5 million default judgment against pirate library WeLib. The site allegedly copied its code and most of its collection from Anna’s Archive, which lost a nearly identical case in May. Ironically, the publishers’ brief appears to ‘copy’ from Anna’s Archive as well, or at least from their own lawsuit against the shadow library.”

item.title: Two characters open up a world of typosquatting opportunities in Chromium browsers
item.description: The Register: “According to Ian Muscat and Leanne Briffa of Have I Been Squatted, there are still characters available to cyber-imposters that can reliably fool web users into trusting URLs that they certainly should not. The latest glyphs bypassing browser safety checks allow tricksters to run websites from a clearly fake domain name (when displayed in Punycode), although they appear just like the real deal in Unicode.”

item.title: Critical internet software is still maintained by just 1 or 2 people
item.description: Coywolf: “A new analysis from sheets.works, The people holding up the internet, reveals that in 2026, key pieces of software the internet depends on are still underfunded or don’t receive any public funding at all. Many of those critical components are kept alive and updated by individual contributors, and it’s often just one or two people.”

item.title: Türkiye documents nearly 7,000 historic tombstones, inscriptions
item.description: Daily Sabah: “The Culture and Tourism Ministry has documented nearly 7,000 tombstones and inscriptions bearing traces of the Turkish-Islamic civilization as part of a nationwide project that expanded from four provinces in 2025 to 18 in 2026. Launched in 2024, the National Inventory Project for Tombstones and Inscriptions of the Turkish-Islamic Period aims to record Anatolia’s historical and cultural heritage through scientific methods and bring the findings together in a comprehensive national digital database.”

item.title: ‘An amazing ride’: SpaceX flight led by first Black female commander sets US speed record
item.description: The Guardian: “Four astronauts pulled up at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday after launching on an eight-hour express that set a US speed record, and that created further history with the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. SpaceX launched commander Jessica Watkins and her crew for Nasa after a three-week delay to fix their Dragon capsule’s leaking fuel system.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Introducing the ACE Research Database: A New, Searchable Collection of Farmed and Wild Animal Advocacy Research
item.description: Animal Charity Evaluators: “Our guiding line is simple: if research has the potential to be useful to farmed and wild animal advocates, we want it in the Database. This ranges from peer-reviewed studies, review articles, and meta-analyses to research reports and theoretical pieces from within the animal advocacy movement.”

item.title: Indiana Landmarks makes more than 100 Black Hoosier oral histories available
item.description: Indiana Landmarks: “More than 100 oral history interviews documenting the experiences, memories, and community histories of Black Hoosiers are now accessible through the Indiana Landmarks Black Heritage Preservation Program’s growing digital oral history collection.”

item.title: EU Commission is in dialogue with Google, spokesperson says
item.description: Reuters: “The European Commission said on Wednesday ​it was ‘in dialogue with Google’ over actions the company ‌may take in response to the $1 billion fines imposed by the EU in July and required changes to its app store and its ​search engine.”

item.title: Van Gogh Museum secures future after resolving dispute with Dutch government
item.description: Museums Journal: “The future of the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam has been secured after the museum and the Dutch Ministry of Education, Culture and Science reached a settlement over funding for a major renovation. The agreement follows a long-running dispute over government support for the project, which had raised questions about whether the museum would be able to carry out the work needed to keep its building safe and suitable for its collection.”

item.title: Ahead of the midterms, Meta has paid at least 29 anti-LGBTQ accounts for their posts
item.description: The 19th: “…after reviewing Meta’s monetization data, Uncloseted Media identified 29 accounts with histories of anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric that have been invited to the program. These include the three aforementioned accounts as well as podcaster Candace Owens, who has blamed gay men for child abuse in the Catholic church, and Turning Point USA, which has been connected to an assault on a queer Arizona State University professor. Meta did not respond to Uncloseted Media and The 19th’s requests for an interview or for comment.”

item.title: YouTube is reportedly gearing up to offer audiobooks
item.description: Engadget: “YouTube is preparing to launch an audiobooks feature as soon as next year and has been in talks with publishers over the previous months, according to the Wall Street Journal. You can already find a bunch of channels with audiobook videos on the platform if you look. Some of them feature titles in the public domain, but some of them offer books that aren’t legally supposed to be on YouTube.”

item.title: How ChatGPT Targets Ads To You Based On Your Prompts, Phone Number, and Email
item.description: 404 Media: “OpenAI lets anyone inject ads into ChatGPT users’ sessions, targeting specific groups of people based on their email address, phone number, or a unique identifier on their phone, according to 404 Media’s own tests of ChatGPT’s advertising ecosystem.”

item.title: Brazil’s Lula accuses Meta of election interference
item.description: AFP: “The campaign of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva accused tech giant Meta of election interference on Saturday after his social media content was allegedly blocked on the company’s platforms.”

item.title: How proposed cuts to this major national health survey could disadvantage Americans with disabilities
item.description: Associated Press: “The federal government is planning to dramatically shrink its most influential health survey, and some researchers worry that the changes will underestimate how many Americans are disabled. At least half the survey questions could be axed. The cost-saving change is part of an ongoing effort to slim down the 69-year-old National Health Interview Survey, which for years has been suffering from declining response rates.”

item.title: How the ‘digital duty of care’ bill could undermine vital sex and drug education online
item.description: The Conversation: “This week the Australian government will introduce its landmark Digital Duty of Care Bill to parliament. The bill aims to make platforms legally responsible for creating a ‘safe online environment’ protecting users from ‘seriously harmful material and conduct’. In the wake of recent controversies – including lawsuits in the United States accusing powerful platforms such as Meta of not doing enough to protect their users – this looks like a long overdue correction. But it’s not that simple.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: The AI Data Center Boom Is Causing a Gigantic Spike in Smog-Spewing Gas Power Plants
item.description: Futurism: “According to a new analysis by the Environment America Research and Policy Center, first flagged by Electrek, the buildout of more AI infrastructure will come with a 44 percent increase in gas-fired generator capacity over the next four years. That’s a stunning rise of nearly 20 gigawatts by 2030, compared to the country’s current gas generator capacity of 41.8 gigawatts, a milestone which took centuries of development — and untold tons of carbon exhaust — to reach.”

item.title: Advocates: Even in Mississippi, data center opposition spans political spectrum. But are politicians listening?
item.description: Mississippi Today: “Even though communities across the state are resoundingly rejecting data centers, very few officials are responsive to the concerns of these communities. Who even asked for these data centers, anyway? What regular citizen wants these data centers in their backyards? Rather, it’s the politicians and corporations telling us from on high that we should want these data centers and they will be good economic opportunities. The divergence between the people and the state is stark.”

item.title: Modi wants India to power the AI age. Residents are pushing back
item.description: Reuters: “India holds 4% of the world’s freshwater for 18% of ​its people, and data centres are clustering in cities already short of it. S&P Global estimates 60% to 80% of Indian data centres could face high water stress this decade. In 2025, data centres used about 150 billion litres ​of water, a figure projected to more than double by 2030, according to research firm Mordor Intelligence.”

item.title: Texas agency sues to stop release of data center records that it says could aid terrorists
item.description: Texas Tribune: “The Public Utility Commission of Texas is asking a Travis County judge to block the release of information showing where data centers and virtual currency mines operate, saying those details could aid terrorists. The lawsuit…pits the state agency responsible for regulating utilities against Attorney General Ken Paxton’s office over the scope of Texas’ public-records law and the state’s protections for critical infrastructure.”

item.title: Proposed mega data center in Silicon Valley raises energy and environmental concerns
item.description: Spectrum Local News: “The potential impact on electricity rates and who should pay for major grid upgrades are at the center of a California Public Utilities Commission review of an agreement between utility company PG&E and Google to connect a massive 250-megawatt data center in San Jose.”

item.title: Google’s Gemini Argon 4 Is Now Available Worldwide
item.description: Gizmodo: “For now, Argon is only accessible to paying customers through the API in AI Studio, Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers via the Gemini App, and Antigravity, Google’s agentic software development platform. It’s currently priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, but those rates will double starting in December.”

item.title: Exclusive: AI safety money floods into political races
item.description: Axios: “Advocates for AI safety and regulation are emerging as a force in U.S. elections, spending nearly $50 million this election cycle on candidates who favor regulation, a new analysis shared exclusively with Axios shows.”

item.title: Denver’s AI chatbot ‘Sunny’ may sunset after council rejects contract
item.description: Denver Post: “Denver’s artificial intelligence chatbot ‘Sunny’ is on track to power down after the City Council rejected a contract Tuesday with the company that operates the service. Councilmembers argued that the program often provides inaccurate information and eliminates jobs that humans should have.”

item.title: Germany moves to criminalize sexual deepfakes and rape videos
item.description: Politico: “The German government has approved a draft law on digital violence Wednesday in a bid to tighten the rules on rape videos and pornographic deepfakes. The possession and production of videos depicting rape are currently not prohibited in Germany if intended for private use, while there is no specific law which regulates using sexual deepfakes of a particular person, according to press agency dpa.”

item.title: Lost generation: the AI threat to Britain’s next great directors
item.description: The Guardian: “The advertising industry has long been a breeding ground for British film and TV talent who have gone on to make the jump to Hollywood productions, including Guy Ritchie, who started out making music videos and commercials, and Paddington in Peru director Dougal Wilson, whose credits include a number of John Lewis’s famous Christmas ads. But the panicked race to introduce AI technology across the advertising industry, to cut client costs and avoid being pushed aside by big tech, has raised fears of a lost generation who may be denied the opportunity to develop into great British film and TV directors.”

item.title: Is It a Relationship if No One’s on the Other Side?
item.description: New York Times: “[Sherry] Turkle’s latest book, ‘Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines,’ turns this lens on A.I. So I wanted to have her on the show to help me figure out what’s going on now that talking machines have very much arrived, what it means that so many of us are building these — I don’t know, call it relationships; don’t call it relationships — with them, and what might happen if we keep going down this path.”

item.title: McDonald’s sued over AI tool that recommends prices to US franchisees
item.description: Associated Press: “The lawsuit, which was filed Friday in Illinois, said McDonald’s pricing tool uses artificial intelligence to collect data that competing franchises wouldn’t normally share, like store-level sales. The Chicago-based burger giant has said it makes the tool available to U.S. franchisees to help them set prices at their individual restaurants. The lawsuit also blames the pricing system for raising McDonald’s U.S. prices.”

item.title: AI training of copyrighted material not fair use: Third Circuit
item.description: Courthouse News Service: “The Third Circuit rejected an artificial intelligence company’s fair use defense after it trained its AI on a competitor’s product, finding the training constituted copyright infringement — and potentially setting a landmark precedent for artificial intelligence.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: New guide: Green computing for software developers
item.description: Institute for Research Software: “The guide is aimed at researchers and software developers who want to understand the environmental impact of their computing and take practical steps to reduce it. It explores how everyday decisions about writing code, testing software and using computing resources can help reduce energy use and carbon emissions.”

item.title: Pentagon Names One of Its Own Public Affairs Officials to Run Stars and Stripes
item.description: Military.com: “The Pentagon has named one of its own public affairs officials to run the publication Stars and Stripes, and he will keep his Pentagon job while doing it. This places a single official inside both the office that shapes the military’s message, and the newsroom charged with covering it independently. Christian Devine, an executive director and principal adviser in the Pentagon’s public affairs office, was appointed acting publisher by chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell.”

item.title: Feds reveal timeline for closure of National Archives in SF
item.description: AsAm News: “The National Archives is doubling down on its intention to close its immigration records facility near San Francisco and move the archives to Kansas.”

item.title: Trump’s Truth Social sees drop in users despite his constant posting
item.description: The Independent: “Truth Social’s traffic fell more than 30 percent over the past year, according to data from digital intelligence firm Similarweb. The social media platform averaged about 260,000 daily users last month, a sharp drop from its peak of 420,000 in June 2025.”

item.title: X purges 13,000 accounts linked to suspected meddling ahead of US midterms
item.description: The Register: “X says it has nuked more than 13,000 accounts involved in three suspected foreign influence operations targeting US political debate. In a post on Wednesday evening, the platform linked the operations to Iran, Russia, and China. It said the networks used inauthentic accounts to post and amplify political content targeting candidates and public figures across the political spectrum.”

item.title: YouTuber Says Cops Paid Him a Visit After He Built Flock-Style Camera to Track Cops
item.description: Gizmodo: “It’s little surprise…that police might be leery of having ALPR devices pointed at them: they know only too well how the data gathered by these devices can be, and is, misused. This point was demonstrated recently by Canadian software engineer and YouTuber Anthony Sistilli, of Brampton, Ontario, a city that recently spent 2 million Canadian dollars on ‘high-resolution cameras, along with automated licence plate recognition technology.’ A month or so ago, Sistilli built his own ALPR camera and set it up to track the movement of police cars.”

item.title: Global finance leaders discuss Bangkok Blueprint on digital fraud
item.description: The Nation (Thailand): “The Bangkok Blueprint for Fraud-Resilient Financial Services was officially launched in Thailand on Wednesday (October 14, 2026), during the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG). The report provides a global strategic framework to prevent, detect and respond to rapidly expanding cyber-enabled fraud linked to transnational organised crime.”

item.title: YouTube Overtakes TV as Top Source of Political News, Study Finds
item.description: Syracuse University: “Social media is now a core news source for Americans: 59% access general news from social media often or always and 55% get political information there at the same rate. Reliance runs highest among younger adults and those that identify as African Americans and Republicans. YouTube ranks as the single most-used platform for political and election news at 16.5%, closely followed by broadcast and cable TV news (16.1%) and print and online news sites (15.7%).”

item.title: A Cray-1 supercomputer replica from 30 “obsolete” Mac Minis
item.description: Ars Technica: “The Museo de Historia de la Computación in Spain has unveiled a 1:1 scale visual replica of the famous Cray-1 supercomputer from 1976. Instead of sourcing expensive, cutting-edge tech to run the system, the creative team powered the project with 30 2012-era Mac Minis. Developed over 18 months, the project serves as a 50th-anniversary tribute to the Cray-1 and Apple’s founding.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: New interactive Alaska tsunami hazard map helps communities prepare
item.description: University of Alaska Fairbanks: “Alaska has 6,700 miles of coastline, including its islands, and much of it is vulnerable to a devastating tsunami. The tsunami hazard tool aims to help the public understand the danger and know what to do and where to go when a tsunami alert is issued. The map is part of the Alaska Earthquake Center’s expanded tsunami resource page.”

item.title: Nebraska teams with USGS to create new statewide surface geologic map
item.description: University of Nebraska-Lincoln: “To create a statewide Nebraska surficial geologic map with new, more accurate lines showing alluvial contours and other dimensions, the two undertook a massive set of meticulous scientific work. In coordination with the U.S. Geological Survey, they reconciled a wide-ranging patchwork of cartographic information to produce the first-ever statewide map showing Nebraska’s surficial geology. The map, available for the first time at a consistent statewide scale, fills in longstanding cartographic gaps while noting limitations on available evidence in specific cases.”

item.title: Mayor Mamdani Launches NYC Mental Health Connect, Helping New Yorkers Find and Access Local Mental Health Services
item.description: City of New York: “Funded through the New York State Office of Mental Health (OMH), Mental Health Connect allows New Yorkers to explore behavioral health services from over 600 providers based on type of service, appointment availability, ages served, languages spoken, and insurance types accepted — all through a brief questionnaire.”

item.title: “Free map of every DC traffic camera and how often it tickets”
item.description: PoPville: “‘Dear PoPville, I built a free map of all 317 fixed speed, red-light and stop-sign cameras in DC from DDOT’s open data, and thought it might be of interest. For each camera it shows the stretch of street it watches, the direction of travel, the posted limit and 12 months of ticket counts, refreshed monthly.'”

item.title: New on Google Play: More ways to create, discover, and play
item.description: Google Blog: “Google Play connects you with the apps and games you love. Today, it’s becoming the place you go to connect with the ones that you create, making it possible for anyone with an idea to build a personal app and run it on Google Play. We’re also introducing new ways to discover and play that put you in control.”

item.title: Web of Markdown
item.description: Spotted in my RSS feeds: “On October 6, 2026, Dave Winer posted “The web of Markdown” on Scripting News. He imagines a Markdown web browser: no CSS and no frameworks, just Markdown files, as a way to restart the web in 2026….This list is a look at how much of that web already exists among the sites in Dave’s blogroll.”

item.title: Feminist orgs claim Meta censoring posts about Cornell 7 case
item.description: Mashable: “The civil lawsuit claiming that Jane Doe was drugged and raped by seven Chi Phi fraternity members at Cornell University has caused an eruption of content on social media, from the ‘I am Jane Doe’ campaign to help conceal the woman’s identity to celebrities like Florence Pugh posting about the allegations. Now, a coalition of feminist and tech justice organizations claim Meta is censoring content about the case.”

item.title: Ukraine says SpaceX limits Starlink operations, disrupting military
item.description: Reuters: ” SpaceX has introduced a limit on some Starlink services in ‌Ukraine, disrupting combat drone missions for which the technology is crucial, officials said on Wednesday. The satellite internet terminals from Elon Musk’s company are vital for guiding Ukraine’s longer-range drone strikes in occupied southern and ​eastern Ukraine, which have wreaked havoc on Russian logistics.”

item.title: My son killed himself after falling victim to an online scam. I heard it happen – and vowed to protect other children
item.description: The Guardian: “Gavin Guffey was 17 when he was targeted by a ‘sextortionist’ on Instagram. His father Brandon has spent four years fighting for justice, and for social media companies to do more to safeguard young users.”

item.title: Introducing The Garlic-Powered Door And Window Sensor
item.description: Hackaday: “The research article is sadly paywalled, but the IEEE Spectrum article covers all the salient details. The sensor uses ground up garlic peel for the positive side of this triboelectric nanogenerator (TENG) as they call it, with a sheet of polyethylene (PE) forming the negative side. Once installed on a door frame, opening said door generates about 210 VAC with a 45 µA short circuit current. A dual-side layer of garlic peel bumps this up to 400 VAC and 65 µA.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: BeFloodWarned.uk
item.description: Found in my Calishat Snaps: From the About page: “Flooding has historically impacted homes, businesses and communities across the UK, but the number of people affected, and the severity of its impact are growing due to climate change. More intense storms, sudden heavy downpours, and rising sea levels all increase our risk…. BeFloodWarned provides information about local rainfall and current weather and flood warnings. Our sister site BeFloodReady provides more information about Property Flood Resilience (PFR) measures you can install, and how to be better prepared for flooding.”

item.title: Getty Images plans bankruptcy filing, to go private
item.description: Reuters: “Getty Images said on Monday it would file for bankruptcy and go private after a restructuring ​agreement that the visual-content provider expects to close by the ‌end of the year.”

item.title: Russian bot farms are still trolling, even after Ukraine’s drone strikes on Yandex
item.description: The Verge: “Social media users have claimed they’ve noticed less traffic on posts by MAGA-affiliated accounts, as well as those associated with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. Some have even said they’ve noticed a steep drop in spam calls and messages. But these people are wrong. The drone strikes appear to have affected Yandex’s web crawlers, not any disinformation or political operations.”

item.title: UK media regulator says concerns persist over X’s handling of illegal content
item.description: Channel News Asia: “Britain’s media regulator Ofcom said on Wednesday it remained concerned about Elon Musk-owned X’s handling of illegal hate and terrorism-related content despite improvements in response times, while disclosing new restrictions on the Grok AI chatbot.”

item.title: ‘SNL’ Sets Druski as First Online Content Creator to Host
item.description: Variety: “Comedian and internet personality Druski will host the Nov. 7 episode of ‘Saturday Night Live.’ Druski, aka Drew Desbordes, will be the first online creator to host the sketch show. Variety confirmed the news with multiple sources, though reps for ‘SNL’ did not immediately respond to a request for comment and a rep for Druski declined to comment.”

item.title: Family of man killed by tiger criticise online content after Trump reposts video
item.description: The Guardian: “William Chapman, 23, was mauled to death after entering an enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, on Saturday. His family described him as ‘bright, warm and engaging’ and suffering from severe mental illness. They said online footage being shared was ‘deeply offensive’ and causing them ‘severe distress’.”

item.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
item.description: Krebs On Security: “Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.”

item.title: How Greece’s under-15 social media ban will work on Facebook, Instagram and TikTok
item.description: Protothema: “Greece’s new restrictions on children’s access to social media will come into effect on 1 January 2027, Minister of State Akis Skertsos, Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis and Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence Minister Dimitris Papastergiou announced. According to Skertsos, the bill, which has already been submitted to Parliament, is expected to be passed on Thursday, 22 October.”

item.title: Aerospace company accuses digital library service of housing trade secrets
item.description: Courthouse News Service: “A global aerospace and defense supplier sued Scribd Monday, accusing the digital library service of knowingly disseminating trade secrets. Honeywell Aerospace accuses Scribd, a digital document library where users have uploaded over 300 million files, of hosting and distributing highly sensitive technical publications and manuals in violation of the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act and the Delaware Uniform Trade Secrets Act.”

item.title: When No ID Means No Internet: Age Verification and the Right to Access Information
item.description: EFF: “Age verification proposals are often presented as a simple tradeoff: sacrifice a little privacy to better safeguard children online. But that framing overlooks a more fundamental question. What happens to people who cannot verify their age at all? This is particularly a problem when users are required to prove their age with identity documents. Age-related restrictions are developing quickly around the world. While they differ radically across jurisdictions, in the past year, we’ve witnessed a sharp uptick toward mandatory age assurance for social media access but also for other high-risk digital services.”

item.title: Thousands of textile treasures preserved in new project
item.description: BBC: “A treasure trove of thousands of items in storage for decades at a mill museum in Lancashire are being checked for the first time and added to a new database. Helmshore Mills Textile Museum has helped preserve Lancashire’s textile industry history for the past 40 years. As textile firms collapsed in the 1960s and 70s, many contents of mills were scrapped or sold but the Lancashire Museum Service saved items and stored them at the Helmshore museum.”

item.title: USU Offers Virtual Campus Experience Through Roblox
item.description: Utah State University: “Launched in Fall 2026, the USU Experience — known as Aggie Campus Life — challenges users to ‘earn’ their degree across three colleges through daily interactive activities. Players can explore inside campus buildings, snap a photo with Big Blue, and dive into Aggie traditions, preparing the next generation of students through hands-on design and immersive play.” Good morning, Internet…
